decks.title: The Age of Industrialisation — Part 1: Before and During the Industrial Revolution in Britain
goals: Explain proto-industrialisation and the roles of town merchants and rural producers
Describe how factories came up in Britain and why the pace of change was slow
Explain why hand labour persisted and how industrialisation affected workers' lives

slides.heading: The Age of Industrialisation
slides.body_md: Part 1 — production **before factories**, the **first factories**, and why **hand labour** survived in Britain. *School periodic assessment only: this chapter is not examined in the CBSE board paper.*

nodes.label: Production before factories
Why merchants went to villages
The first factories
A slow revolution
Hand labour and workers' lives

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: production before factories, why merchants went to villages, the first factories, a slow revolution, and hand labour and workers' lives
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Namaste! When we hear the words industrial revolution, we imagine smoking chimneys and huge machines. But the real story is slower and more surprising. Long before factories, villages were already producing goods for distant markets, and even after factories came, hand labour stayed important. Note that your school tests this chapter in periodic assessment; it is not part of the board paper.

slides.heading: Production before factories
slides.body_md: Historians call this phase **proto-industrialisation**: large-scale production for world markets, **without factories**.

rows: Where
Mostly in rural homes, not factories
For whom
An international market
Organised by
Town merchants who gave advances and raw materials
Done by
Peasant and artisan families, using the labour of all members
Alongside
Farming on small plots

visual.alt: Table of features of the proto-industrial system: production mostly in rural homes for an international market, organised by town merchants, done by peasant families with family labour, alongside farming

slides.narration: Before factories, Europe already produced goods on a large scale for an international market. But the work happened in village homes. Merchants from towns gave money and raw material to peasant families, who spun and wove at home, using the labour of every family member, while still farming their small plots. Historians call this early phase proto-industrialisation.

slides.heading: Why did merchants go to the villages?

nodes.label: World trade and colonies expand: demand for goods rises
Town guilds restrict new producers and control prices
Merchants turn to the countryside
Peasants, short of land after enclosures, take up work at home

visual.alt: Flow: rising demand from world trade and colonies, restrictions by town guilds, merchants turning to the countryside, and land-short peasants taking up work at home
visual.caption: Why production moved to villages

slides.narration: Why villages? As world trade and colonies grew, demand for goods rose. But in towns, powerful guilds of craftsmen controlled production. They trained workers, fixed prices, limited competition and kept out newcomers, often with special rights from rulers. So merchants could not expand in towns. They turned to the countryside, where poor peasants were looking for extra work.

slides.heading: Why did peasants agree?

rows: Common lands enclosed: no free grazing or firewood
A new source of cash income
Small plots could not feed the family
Extra earnings without leaving the village
Idle hands in the slack farm season
Work for women, children and men at home

visual.alt: Table of rural problems and how merchant work helped: enclosure of commons, small plots and idle seasons were offset by cash income, extra earnings at home and work for the whole family

slides.narration: The peasants had their own reasons. Open common lands, where they once grazed animals and gathered firewood, were being enclosed. Their own plots were too small to feed the family. Work from the merchant brought cash income without leaving the village, and it kept women, children and men busy in the slack farm season. So the arrangement suited both sides.

slides.body_md: A merchant leaves wool with a village family; they spin and weave at home and still farm. What is this?
slides.narration: Look at where the work happens, who organises it, and whether there is a factory.

slides.heading: A network controlled from the town

nodes.label: Merchant in town buys raw material
Rural families spin and weave
Finishing workshop in a town
Merchant exports the cloth

visual.alt: Flow of a town-controlled network: a merchant buys raw material, rural families spin and weave, a town workshop finishes the cloth, and the merchant exports it
visual.caption: Controlled from the town, produced in the countryside

slides.narration: Notice how the system worked. The merchant lived in a town, but the work was done in many village homes. He bought raw material, passed it to spinners and then weavers, sent the cloth to a town workshop for finishing, and then sold it abroad. The producers were scattered and many, but the merchant controlled every link in the chain. Town and countryside were tied together.

slides.narration: Here is how to turn this into a three-mark answer. First, the meaning: production for a world market before factories. Second, how it worked: town merchants and rural families. Third, why it developed: guilds in towns, and poor peasants in villages. Three distinct points, one per mark, in about sixty words. That shape works for most three-mark history questions.

slides.heading: The coming of the factory

rows: Earliest English factories (from the 1730s)
Few at first; they multiplied only in the late 18th century
New machines (carding, twisting, spinning)
Each stage of cotton production became faster
Richard Arkwright's cotton mill
Costly machines and all stages under one roof and one management
Result
Close supervision, quality control and regulation of labour

visual.alt: Table of how factories came up in England: early factories from the 1730s, new spinning machines, Arkwright's mill bringing all stages under one roof, and closer supervision and quality control

slides.narration: The earliest factories in England appeared around the seventeen thirties, but they multiplied only towards the end of that century. Cotton led the way. New machines speeded up every stage of cotton production. Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill, bringing costly machines and all the stages under one roof and one management. Now owners could supervise workers, check quality and control the pace of work.

slides.heading: A slow revolution

rows: Cotton led until the 1840s; then iron and steel grew with railways
Only a few sectors changed fast
Most workers stayed in traditional industries (food, building, pottery, glass, tanning, furniture)
Change came through small innovations
Watt's improved steam engine (patented 1781) found few buyers for years
New machines were costly and unreliable

visual.alt: Table on the slow pace of change: cotton then iron and steel led, most workers stayed in traditional industries, and the steam engine spread slowly because machines were costly and unreliable

slides.narration: Did factories take over overnight? No. Cotton led until the eighteen forties, and then iron and steel grew with the railways. But most workers stayed in traditional industries like food processing, building and pottery, which changed through small improvements. New machines were expensive and often broke down. Even James Watt's improved steam engine, patented in seventeen eighty one, found few buyers for years.

slides.heading: Quick check: the bookbinder
slides.body_md: A London bookbinder has heavy work only before Christmas. Why would he prefer hand labour to machines?
slides.narration: Think about how many months a costly machine would actually be used.

slides.heading: Hand labour or machines?
columns:
**Why Britain kept hand labour**

- Plenty of cheap labour from the countryside
- Seasonal trades needed workers only part of the year
- Buyers wanted many designs and shapes
- The rich preferred handmade goods as a mark of class

**Why America mechanised faster**

- Labour was scarce and costly
- Machines saved money where workers were few
- Large, uniform markets suited machine-made goods
slides.narration: Why did many British industrialists stick with hand labour? Workers were plentiful and cheap, so expensive machines made little sense. Many trades were seasonal. Customers wanted many designs and shapes that machines could not easily make, and the rich valued handmade goods as a sign of class. In America, where workers were scarce, machines paid off sooner. The choice depended on the cost of labour.

slides.heading: Life of the workers

nodes.label: Poor peasants migrate to cities
Jobs found through friends and relatives; many wait for weeks
Seasonal work: long spells without income
Fear of machines; attacks on the spinning jenny
From the 1840s: city building and railways create work

visual.alt: Flow of workers' lives: migration to cities, finding jobs through networks, seasonal unemployment, fear of machines and attacks on the spinning jenny, and new work from city building and railways after the 1840s
visual.caption: Life of workers in industrial Britain

slides.narration: For workers, life was hard. Poor peasants came to the cities, but finding a job depended on knowing someone inside. Many waited for weeks, sleeping under bridges. Work was often seasonal, so long spells passed without income, and rising prices ate into wages. Fear of losing work made workers hostile to machines. After the eighteen forties, building roads, stations and sewers in cities created more work.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: why attack a spinning jenny?
slides.body_md: Explain why some women spinners attacked the spinning jenny (James Hargreaves, 1764).
bullets: Step 1 — Describe the machine: one worker could turn **several spindles** at once.
Step 2 — Effect: **fewer hand-spinners** were needed.
Step 3 — Link to workers: women who lived by spinning feared **losing their income**.
Step 4 — Conclude: fear of **unemployment** made workers hostile to new technology.

rows: The machine
One worker can turn several spindles at once
Effect on demand
Fewer hand-spinners needed for the same yarn
Workers' fear
Women who lived by hand-spinning would lose income
Response
Some attacked the new machines

visual.alt: Table explaining hostility to the spinning jenny: one worker could turn several spindles, fewer hand-spinners were needed, women spinners feared losing income, and some attacked the machines

slides.narration: Cause and effect questions need a chain. The spinning jenny let one worker turn several spindles at once. So fewer spinners were needed for the same yarn. Women who earned their living by spinning by hand saw their income threatened, and some attacked the machines. The general lesson: when jobs were scarce, new technology looked like a threat to workers.

slides.body_md: True or false? In Victorian Britain, the upper classes preferred machine-made goods to handmade ones.
slides.narration: Think about what handmade goods signalled about a family's status.

goals: Explain how British policy and Company control affected Indian weavers
Describe the growth of factories in India and the peculiarities of industrial growth
Explain how advertisements helped create markets for goods

slides.heading: Industrialisation in the colonies: India
slides.body_md: Part 2 — Indian **textiles**, the **weavers** under Company rule, **factories** in India, and the **market for goods**. *School periodic assessment only: this chapter is not examined in the CBSE board paper.*

nodes.label: The age of Indian textiles
Company and the weavers
Manchester comes to India
Factories in India
Small-scale industry
Advertising and markets

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: Indian textiles, the Company and the weavers, Manchester in India, factories in India, small-scale industry, and advertising
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Now we travel to India. Before machines, India was the world's great textile producer. Under colonial rule, weavers lost their markets and their freedom, and Manchester cloth flooded in. Yet Indian factories grew, and handloom weavers survived in surprising ways. We end with how sellers used pictures and slogans to win buyers. Again, this is a school periodic assessment chapter.

slides.heading: The age of Indian textiles

rows: Overland
From Punjab through mountain passes, by camel
Afghanistan, Persia, Central Asia
Western sea trade
Surat (Gujarat)
Gulf and Red Sea ports
Eastern sea trade
Masulipatnam (Coromandel), Hooghly (Bengal)
Southeast Asian ports

visual.alt: Table of pre-colonial routes of Indian textile trade: overland from Punjab to Afghanistan, Persia and Central Asia; Surat to the Gulf and Red Sea; Masulipatnam and Hooghly to Southeast Asia

slides.narration: Before machine industry, Indian silk and cotton goods dominated the world's textile trade, especially the finer varieties. Bales of cloth went overland from Punjab, on camels through mountain passes, to Afghanistan, Persia and Central Asia. By sea, Surat on the Gujarat coast linked India to the Gulf and the Red Sea, while Masulipatnam and Hooghly traded with Southeast Asia.

slides.heading: Who ran the export trade?

nodes.label: Weavers in villages
Supply merchants give advances and collect cloth
Brokers at the port
Export merchants and shippers
Overseas buyers

visual.alt: Flow of the pre-colonial export network: village weavers, supply merchants giving advances, port brokers, export merchants and shippers, and overseas buyers
visual.caption: Financed and run by Indian merchants and bankers

slides.narration: A whole network of Indian merchants and bankers ran this trade. Supply merchants gave advances to weavers in the villages, collected the woven cloth and carried it to the ports. At the ports, brokers bargained with them on behalf of the big export merchants and shippers. Credit, goods and information flowed through this network, and weavers could sell to more than one buyer.

slides.heading: A network breaks down

rows: Indian merchants and bankers control the network
European companies win concessions, then monopoly rights
Surat and Hooghly thrive
Surat and Hooghly decline; credit dries up
Many old trading houses
Bombay and Calcutta grow; trade in European ships

visual.alt: Table of the shift after the 1750s: from Indian-controlled trade through Surat and Hooghly to European company control through Bombay and Calcutta

slides.narration: From the seventeen fifties, this network began to break down. European companies first won trading concessions from local rulers and then monopoly rights. The old ports of Surat and Hooghly declined as their trade shrank and credit dried up. The new ports of Bombay and Calcutta grew, but trade through them was controlled by European companies and carried in European ships.

slides.narration: Look back at the table of routes and ports.

slides.heading: The Company and the weavers

nodes.label: East India Company gains political power (from the 1760s)
Removes old traders and brokers
Appoints gomasthas to supervise weavers
Advances tie weavers to sell only to the Company
Low prices, harassment, loss of bargaining power

visual.alt: Flow of Company control: political power from the 1760s, removal of traders and brokers, gomasthas supervising weavers, advances tying weavers to the Company, and low prices and loss of bargaining power
visual.caption: How the Company controlled weavers

slides.narration: After the East India Company gained political power in Bengal from the seventeen sixties, it wanted cloth cheaply and without competition. It pushed out the old traders and brokers. It appointed gomasthas, paid servants who supervised weavers and checked the cloth. And it gave advances: once a weaver took the loan, he had to sell his cloth only to the gomastha, at a price the Company fixed.

slides.heading: How weavers responded

rows: Deserted villages
Moved with their looms to villages of relatives
Revolts
With village traders, opposed the Company and its officials
Refused advances
Closed workshops; many became agricultural labourers

visual.alt: Table of weavers' responses to Company control: deserting villages, revolting with village traders, and refusing advances to become agricultural labourers

slides.narration: Weavers did not simply accept this. Gomasthas were outsiders who often came with armed men and punished weavers for delays. In many villages of the Carnatic and Bengal, weavers left with their looms to settle in the villages of relatives. Elsewhere, they joined village traders in revolts. Over time, many refused advances, closed their workshops and became farm labourers.

slides.heading: Manchester comes to India

nodes.label: British cotton industry grows
Duties in Britain keep Indian cloth out
Manchester cloth sold in India
Weavers lose export and home markets
1860s: American Civil War makes raw cotton scarce and costly
Late 19th century: Indian mills add competition

visual.alt: Flow of the weavers' troubles: British industry grows, duties keep Indian cloth out of Britain, Manchester cloth is sold in India, weavers lose markets, raw cotton becomes costly in the 1860s, and Indian mills add competition
visual.caption: Manchester comes to India

slides.narration: In the early eighteen hundreds, a bigger blow came. As Britain's cotton industry grew, it put duties on Indian cloth to keep it out, while Manchester cloth was sold in India. Weavers lost both their export market and much of their home market, because machine-made cloth was cheaper. In the eighteen sixties the American Civil War made raw cotton scarce and costly. Then Indian mills added more competition.

slides.narration: History answers become easier with a timeline. First, the Company gains power in the seventeen sixties. Then gomasthas and advances take away the weavers' freedom. In the early nineteenth century, British duties and cheap Manchester cloth take away their markets. In the eighteen sixties raw cotton becomes costly, and finally Indian mills compete too. Each step made the next one worse.

slides.heading: Factories come up in India

rows: First cotton mill in Bombay
First jute mill in Bengal

visual.alt: Table of early factories in India: first cotton mill in Bombay 1854, first jute mill in Bengal 1855, Kanpur and Ahmedabad mills in the 1860s, Madras mill 1874, Tata steel at Jamshedpur 1912

slides.narration: Indian factories began in the eighteen fifties. The first cotton mill came up in Bombay in eighteen fifty four, and the first jute mill in Bengal a year later. Mills followed in Kanpur and Ahmedabad in the eighteen sixties, and in Madras in eighteen seventy four. In nineteen twelve, steel production began at Jamshedpur. Mill towns grew around these factories.

slides.heading: Who invested, and who controlled?

headers: How they gathered capital or controlled industry
rows: Dwarkanath Tagore (Bengal)
Fortune from the China trade; invested in joint-stock companies
Parsi merchants of Bombay, e.g. Jamsetji Tata
Exports to China and raw cotton shipments to England
Seth Hukumchand (Marwari)
Set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta (1917); China trade
European managing agencies (e.g. Andrew Yule)
Raised capital and controlled tea, coffee, mining, indigo and jute

visual.alt: Table of early industrial capital in India: Dwarkanath Tagore and Parsi merchants from the China and cotton trade, Seth Hukumchand's jute mill in 1917, and European managing agencies controlling plantations, mining, indigo and jute

slides.narration: Where did the money come from? Many early Indian industrialists made fortunes in trade with China. Dwarkanath Tagore of Bengal and Parsi merchants of Bombay such as Jamsetji Tata are examples, and Seth Hukumchand set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta in nineteen seventeen. But colonial rule limited Indian merchants, and European managing agencies controlled large sectors, mainly for export.

slides.heading: Where did the workers come from?

nodes.label: Peasants and artisans leave villages for mill towns
Crowds wait at the mill gate
Jobber recruits men from his village
Jobber helps them settle but demands gifts and money

visual.alt: Flow: peasants and artisans move to mill towns, crowds wait at mill gates, the jobber recruits men from his village and helps them but demands gifts and money
visual.caption: Getting a mill job

slides.narration: Mill workers came mostly from nearby districts: peasants and artisans who could not find work at home. Many returned to their villages for harvests and festivals. Jobs were scarce, so crowds waited at the gates. Mill owners used jobbers, trusted older workers who brought men from their own villages. The jobber helped newcomers settle, but he also demanded money and gifts, and gained power over their lives.

slides.body_md: An old, trusted worker brings men from his village, finds them jobs and demands gifts. Who is he?
slides.narration: This person belongs to Indian mill towns, not to the Company's weaving villages.

slides.heading: The peculiar pattern of growth

nodes.label: Late 19th century: Indian mills make coarse yarn for handlooms and China
From 1905: swadeshi boycott of foreign cloth
From 1906: yarn exports to China fall
Mills shift from yarn to cloth
1914–18: war cuts Manchester imports; Indian mills grow

visual.alt: Flow of changes in Indian industry: coarse yarn for handlooms and China, swadeshi boycott from 1905, falling yarn exports to China from 1906, a shift from yarn to cloth, and growth during the First World War
visual.caption: How the pattern of industry changed

slides.narration: Indian industrial growth followed a peculiar path. Early cotton mills made coarse yarn, not cloth, for Indian handloom weavers and for China. From nineteen oh five, the swadeshi movement urged people to boycott foreign cloth. Yarn exports to China fell from nineteen oh six, so mills shifted to making cloth. Then the First World War cut Manchester imports, and Indian mills, with army orders, grew fast.

slides.heading: Small-scale industry and the handloom

rows: Large factories were a small part of industry
Most production stayed in small and household units
Handloom output expanded in the 20th century
Weavers survived, especially in fine and special cloth
Fly shuttle
Ropes and pulleys pass the weft quickly: more output, wider cloth

visual.alt: Table on small-scale industry: large factories were a small part of industry, handloom output expanded in the twentieth century, and the fly shuttle raised weavers' output

slides.narration: Even so, large factories were only a small part of Indian industry. Most production stayed in small workshops and homes, and handloom weaving actually expanded in the twentieth century. New tools helped. The fly shuttle, worked by ropes and pulleys, passed the weft thread quickly, so a weaver could produce more and weave wider cloth. Fine and special saris, which mills could not easily copy, kept weavers going.

slides.heading: Creating a market: advertisements

rows: "Made in Manchester" on cloth labels
Trusted quality
Images of gods and goddesses
The product is blessed and familiar
Calendars in homes, shops and offices
Seen daily, even by people who cannot read
Images of emperors and nawabs
Fit for royalty, so worthy of respect
Swadeshi slogans of Indian mills
Buying Indian goods serves the nation

visual.alt: Table of advertising methods in colonial India and their messages: Made in Manchester labels, images of deities, calendars, royal images and swadeshi slogans

slides.narration: How do you sell new goods to new buyers? With advertisements. Manchester cloth carried labels saying Made in Manchester, a promise of quality. Labels and calendars showed gods and goddesses, or emperors and nawabs, to make products feel blessed or royal. Calendars hung in homes and tea shops reached even people who could not read. Indian manufacturers answered with a swadeshi message: buy Indian, serve the nation.

bullets: Step 1 — Who sells to whom? (a Manchester company to Indian buyers)
Step 2 — What picture and words? (a goddess; "Made in Manchester")
Step 3 — What appeal? (**quality** and **divine approval**)

slides.narration: An advertisement is a historical source. Ask four questions. Who is selling, and to whom? What pictures and words are used? What feeling does it appeal to: quality, faith, status or the nation? And what does it tell us about its time? A Manchester label with a goddess tells us that foreign sellers were working hard to win Indian buyers.

slides.narration: Here is Part 2 in brief. Indian textiles once led the world. Under the Company, gomasthas and advances took away weavers' freedom, and Manchester cloth took their markets. Factories grew from eighteen fifty four, financed partly by China-trade fortunes, with jobbers recruiting workers. Swadeshi and the First World War helped Indian industry, handlooms survived, and advertisements shaped what people bought.

slides.heading: Tips for your periodic test: Part 2
bullets: Gomasthas, advances, jobbers: define each and say **whom** they served.
Weavers' decline: give **causes in order** (Company control, Manchester, raw cotton, mills).
Early factories: **Bombay 1854**, **jute in Bengal 1855**, **Madras 1874**, **Jamshedpur 1912**.
First World War: **imports fell**, **war orders** rose, Manchester **never recovered**.
Advertisements: name the **method** and its **message**.
Map practice: Surat, Masulipatnam, Hooghly; Bombay, Ahmedabad, Kanpur.
slides.narration: Last tips. Do not mix up gomasthas, who served the Company in the eighteenth century, with jobbers, who recruited mill workers later. Give the causes of the weavers' decline in order. Learn four dates for early factories. For the First World War, three ideas: imports fell, war orders rose, and Manchester never recovered. And for advertisements, always pair the method with its message.

notes.title: The Age of Industrialisation — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Before the industrial revolution: proto-industrialisation
sections.body_md:
*This chapter is assessed only in school periodic assessment, not in the CBSE board paper.*

Even before factories, England and Europe produced goods on a large scale for an **international market**. This phase is called **proto-industrialisation**.

- **Why merchants went to the countryside:** world trade and colonies raised demand, but in towns, **crafts and trade guilds** (associations of producers that trained craftspeople, controlled production, prices and competition, and kept out newcomers, often with monopoly rights from rulers) blocked expansion.
- **Why peasants agreed:** with **common lands enclosed** and plots too small, poor peasants needed extra income; they could work at home, use **family labour** and keep farming.
- **How it worked:** town merchants gave **advances and raw material**; rural households spun and wove; cloth was finished in towns and exported. Production was scattered, but **merchants controlled** the network, tying town and countryside together.

key_terms.definition_md: Large-scale production for an international market, organised by merchants in rural homes, before factories.
An association of producers that trained craftspeople and controlled production, prices and entry.
Fencing of common lands for private use, which took away a resource of poor peasants.

rows: Where
Mostly in rural homes, not factories
For whom

sections.heading: 3. Hand labour, steam power and the life of workers
sections.body_md:
**Why hand labour persisted in Victorian Britain:** there was **no shortage of labour**, so wages were low and industrialists avoided machines needing large capital; **seasonal trades** (gasworks, breweries, bookbinders, Christmas goods, ship repair in winter) hired hands for the peak; many products needed **varied designs and shapes** that machines could not make; and the **upper classes preferred handmade goods** as a mark of refinement. In **America**, where labour was scarce, industrialists mechanised more eagerly.

**Workers' lives:** finding a job depended on **networks of friends and kin**; many waited for weeks, sleeping under bridges or in night shelters; **seasonal work** meant long periods without income; prices rose, so wages bought less. **Fear of unemployment** made workers hostile to new technology: when the **spinning jenny** (James Hargreaves, 1764) came into the woollen industry, women who lived by hand-spinning attacked the machines. From the **1840s**, city building (roads, railway stations, tunnels, drains) created more work.

sections.heading: 4. Industrialisation in the colonies: the Indian weavers
sections.body_md:
**The age of Indian textiles:** before machine industry, Indian silk and cotton goods **dominated international trade**. Cloth went overland from Punjab to Afghanistan, Persia and Central Asia, and by sea from **Surat** (to the Gulf and Red Sea) and from **Masulipatnam** and **Hooghly** (to Southeast Asia). A network of Indian **supply merchants, brokers and export merchants** financed and ran the trade.

**Breakdown (from the 1750s):** European companies won concessions and then monopoly rights; **Surat and Hooghly declined**; **Bombay and Calcutta** grew, with trade in European ships.

**The Company and the weavers:** after gaining political power (1760s), the Company removed old traders and brokers, appointed **gomasthas** (paid servants who supervised weavers and checked cloth) and used a system of **advances** that tied weavers to sell only to it, at low prices. Weavers clashed with gomasthas; many **deserted villages**, some **revolted**, others **refused advances** and became agricultural labourers.

**Manchester comes to India:** British duties shut out Indian cloth, and cheap **Manchester cloth** flooded India, so weavers lost both export and local markets. In the **1860s**, the **American Civil War** raised raw cotton exports from India and its price, starving weavers of supplies. By the late nineteenth century, **Indian mills** added competition.

sections.heading: 5. Factories in India and the peculiarities of industrial growth
sections.body_md:
**Early factories:** the first **cotton mill in Bombay (1854)**; the first **jute mill in Bengal (1855)**; mills in **Kanpur** (Elgin Mill) and **Ahmedabad** in the 1860s; the first spinning and weaving mill of **Madras (1874)**; **Tata steel at Jamshedpur (1912)**.

**Entrepreneurs:** many made money in the **China trade**: **Dwarkanath Tagore** (Bengal), Parsis of Bombay such as **Dinshaw Petit** and **Jamsetji Tata** (also raw cotton exports to England), **Seth Hukumchand** (first Indian jute mill in Calcutta, 1917). Colonial rule restricted Indian merchants to exporting raw materials, and **European managing agencies** (Bird Heiglers, Andrew Yule, Jardine Skinner) controlled large sectors, especially tea, coffee, mining, indigo and jute for **export**.

**Workers:** mostly from **nearby districts**, moving between village and mill; recruited through **jobbers**, who helped them but demanded money and gifts and gained power over them.

**Peculiarities:** early mills produced **coarse yarn** for handlooms and for **China**; the **swadeshi movement** (from 1905) and the fall of yarn exports to China (from 1906) pushed mills to make **cloth**; the **First World War** cut Manchester imports and brought **war orders**, and Manchester never recovered its position. Yet **small-scale and household units** remained most of industry, and **handloom output expanded**, helped by the **fly shuttle**.

sections.heading: 6. The market for goods
sections.body_md:
New products needed new buyers. **Advertisements** made products seem desirable and necessary and created new needs.

- **Labels** on Manchester cloth said **"Made in Manchester"** to promise quality, and often carried images of **Indian gods and goddesses**, giving the product a sense of divine approval and familiarity.
- **Calendars** carried advertisements into homes, tea shops and offices, reaching even people who could not read.
- Images of **emperors and nawabs** lent products royal prestige.
- Indian manufacturers made advertising a vehicle for **swadeshi**: buying Indian-made goods was presented as serving the nation.

questions.stem_md: The phase of large-scale production for an international market that took place **before factories**, mostly in rural homes, is known as

options.text_md: liberalisation
proto-industrialisation
globalisation
the industrial revolution

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** proto-industrialisation. Historians call this early phase proto-industrialisation ("proto" = first, earliest form). The industrial revolution came later, with factories; liberalisation and globalisation are modern economic terms.

questions.stem_md: Why did merchants in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century England and Europe find it hard to expand production **in towns**?

options.text_md: Towns had no workers at all
Factories in towns had already captured the whole market
Governments had banned all trade in towns
Powerful urban crafts and trade guilds restricted who could produce and controlled competition and prices

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Powerful urban crafts and trade guilds restricted who could produce and controlled competition and prices. Guilds of producers, often holding monopoly rights from rulers, controlled training, production, prices and entry of newcomers, so merchants turned to the countryside. Towns did have workers, factories had not yet appeared, and trade was not banned.

questions.stem_md: Why were many poor peasants in the English countryside willing to work for town merchants?

options.text_md: Common lands were being enclosed and their small plots could not support the family, so they needed extra income
They were forced by law to leave farming completely
Merchants offered them permanent jobs in city factories
They had become rich and wanted to invest in trade

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Common lands were being enclosed and their small plots could not support the family, so they needed extra income. Enclosure of the commons removed a source of livelihood, and small plots were not enough, so rural families welcomed paid work they could do at home while still farming. They were not forced out of farming, there were no factory jobs yet, and they were poor, not rich.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined English village in 1720, a merchant leaves wool with the Taylor family. The mother and daughters spin, the father weaves in winter, and the family still farms its strip of land. This arrangement is an example of

options.text_md: factory production
a trade guild
proto-industrial production
a managing agency

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** proto-industrial production. Production for a merchant, inside a farm household, using family labour, alongside farming, is the proto-industrial system. There is no factory, it is not a guild of town producers, and managing agencies belong to colonial India.

questions.stem_md: Who controlled the network of production and trade in the proto-industrial system?

options.text_md: The rural families who did the spinning and weaving
Factory owners in big industrial cities
Merchants based in towns, who supplied raw material and sold the finished goods
Trade guilds in the villages

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Merchants based in towns, who supplied raw material and sold the finished goods. Production was spread over many rural households, but merchants controlled it: they gave advances and raw materials, moved goods between stages and sold the finished product. Factories came later, and guilds were urban.

questions.stem_md: Explain how and why production for international markets moved to the countryside in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Europe.
questions.solution_md: Two causes on the merchants' side (demand, guilds), one on the peasants' side, then how the system worked and who controlled it.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Rising demand:** expansion of **world trade and colonies** increased demand for goods, especially cloth.
2. **Guild barriers:** in towns, **crafts and trade guilds** restricted production and new producers, often with **monopoly rights** from rulers.
3. **Rural need:** with **commons enclosed** and small plots, poor peasants needed **extra income**.
4. **The system:** town **merchants gave advances and raw material** to rural households, who spun and wove at home using **family labour**.
5. **Control:** merchants linked the stages and sold the goods abroad, so a **town-controlled network** relied on **countryside labour**.

questions.stem_md: An imagined London bookbinder in the 1840s has heavy work only before Christmas and little for the rest of the year. Why would he prefer hand labour to buying machines?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** He could hire workers just for the busy season instead of tying up money in machines used only part of the year. questions.stem_md: Why did some women who lived by hand-spinning attack the spinning jenny when it was introduced in the woollen industry?

options.text_md: The machine was too slow

questions.stem_md: Industrialists in nineteenth-century America were keener on mechanisation than many in Britain. The best explanation is that

options.text_md: America had no raw materials
British law banned machines
American workers refused to use their hands
labour was scarce in America, whereas Britain had plenty of cheap labour

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** labour was scarce in America, whereas Britain had plenty of cheap labour. Where labour is scarce and costly, machines save money; where it is plentiful and cheap, as in Victorian Britain, hand labour stays attractive.

questions.stem_md: In the early nineteenth century, which **two** problems did Indian cotton weavers face as Manchester goods spread?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Their export market collapsed, and the local market was flooded with cheaper machine-made imports. Duties in Britain shut out Indian cloth, and cheap Manchester cloth undersold weavers at home. Indian factories came later and competed with them too.

questions.stem_md: How did the East India Company establish control over Indian weavers, and how did the weavers respond?
questions.solution_md: Three methods of control, then two kinds of response.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Eliminating traders:** after gaining political power from the 1760s, the Company pushed out the **traders and brokers** linked to cloth trade.
2. **Gomasthas:** it appointed paid servants to **supervise weavers**, collect supplies and check quality.
3. **Advances:** weavers who took **loans** for raw material had to sell their cloth only to the gomastha, at **low prices**.
4. **Responses:** weavers in many villages of the **Carnatic and Bengal** **deserted** their villages and set up looms elsewhere; some, with village traders, **revolted**.
5. **Later:** many weavers **refused loans**, closed workshops and became **agricultural labourers**.

questions.stem_md: "In Victorian Britain, hand labour made better business sense than machines." Evaluate this statement.
questions.solution_md: Three supporting reasons, one counter-point, and a judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Agree — cheap labour:** migrants from the countryside made labour **plentiful and cheap**, so machines that needed large capital looked unnecessary.
2. **Agree — seasons:** in **seasonal** trades (gasworks, bookbinding, Christmas goods), hiring hands for the peak was cheaper than idle machines.
3. **Agree — variety:** buyers wanted **many designs and shapes**; machines made standard goods, and the rich preferred **handmade** goods.
4. **But:** in **cotton and metals**, machines raised output and cut costs, and in labour-scarce **America** mechanisation paid off.
5. **Judgement:** for **most British businesses** of the time the statement holds, because of cheap labour and varied demand, though not for every industry.
